exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Particular Term of a Geometric Sequence Given the First Term and Common Ratio

question.text: The first term of a geometric sequence is $32,$ and the common ratio is $-\dfrac{1}{2}.$  The $12$th term of this sequence is
question.explanation:
The first term is $a_1 = 32,$ and the common ratio is $r = -\dfrac{1}{2},$ so we can write the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= 32 \cdot \left( -\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1} \end{align*}

To find the $12$th term, we can use this formula with $n = 12\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} a_n &= 32 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1} \\[5pt] a_{12} & = 32\cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{12-1} \\[5pt] &=32\cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{11} \\[5pt] &=-2^5\cdot \dfrac{1}{2^{11}} \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{2^{6}} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{64} \end{align*}

Therefore, the $12$th term is $a_{12} =\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ -\dfrac{1}{64}}.$

question.text: The first term of a geometric sequence is $-\dfrac{1}{81},$ and the common ratio is $-3.$ The $9$th term of this sequence is
question.explanation:
The first term is $a_1 = -\dfrac{1}{81},$ and the common ratio is $r = -3,$ so we can write the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{81} \cdot (-3)^{n-1} \end{align*}

To find the $9$th term, we can use this formula with $n = 9\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} a_n &= -\dfrac{1}{81}\cdot (-3)^{n-1} \\[5pt] a_{9} & = -\dfrac{1}{81}\cdot (-3)^{9-1} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{81}\cdot (-3)^{8} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{3^4}\cdot 3^{8} \\[5pt] &= -3^4 \\[5pt] &= -81 \end{align*}

Therefore, the $9$th term is $a_{9} = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-81}.$

question.text: Find the equation for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence if the $5$th term is $16$ and the common ratio is $\dfrac 2 3.$
question.explanation:
The common ratio is $r = \dfrac{2}{3},$ so we can start writing the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= a_1 \cdot \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right)^{n-1} \end{align*}

However, we still need to figure out the first term $a_1.$ We know that the $5$th term is $a_5 = 16,$ so we can solve for the first term as follows:

\begin{align*} a_5 & = a_1 \cdot \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right)^{5-1} \\[5pt] 16 & = a_1 \cdot \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right)^4 \\[5pt] 2^4 &= a_1 \cdot \left( \dfrac{2^4}{3^4} \right) \\[5pt] \dfrac{2^4 \cdot 3^4}{2^4} &= a_1 \\[5pt] 3^4 &= a_1\\[5pt] 81 &= a_1 \end{align*}

Now that we know the first term is $a_1=81,$ we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right)^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= 81 \cdot \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right)^{n-1} \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence if the $6$th term is $-\dfrac15$ and the common ratio is $-\dfrac15.$
question.explanation:
The common ratio is $r = -\dfrac{1}{5},$ so we can start writing the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= a_1 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{n-1} \end{align*}

However, we still need to figure out the first term $a_1.$ We know that the $6$th term is $a_6 = -\dfrac{1}{5},$ so we can solve for the first term as follows:

\begin{align*} a_6 &= a_1 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{6-1} \\[5pt] -\dfrac{1}{5} &= a_1 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^5 \\[5pt] -\dfrac{1}{5} &= -a_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^5 \\[5pt] -\dfrac{1}{5} &= -a_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{5^5}\right) \\[5pt] %\dfrac{1}{5} &= \dfrac{a_1}{5^5} \\[5pt] %\dfrac{5^5}{5} &= a_1 \\[5pt] 5^4 &= a_1 \\[5pt] 625 & = a_1 \end{align*}

Now that we know the first term is $a_1 = 625,$ we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= 625 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{n-1} \end{align*}

question.text: If the sixth term of a geometric sequence is $\dfrac{1}{16}$ and the common ratio is $\dfrac{1}{4},$ then the third term of this sequence is
question.explanation:
The common ratio is $r=\dfrac{1}{4},$ so we can start writing the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \\[5pt] & = a_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{n-1} \end{align*}

However, we still need to figure out the first term $a_1.$ We know that the $6$th term is $a_6 = 16,$ so we can solve for the first term as follows:

\begin{align*} a_6 &= a_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{6-1} \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{16} &= a_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^5 \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{4^2} &= a_1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{4^5} \\[5pt] \dfrac{4^5}{4^2} &= a_1 \\[5pt] a_1 &= 64 \end{align*}

Now that we know the first term is $a_1 = 64,$ we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= 64 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{n-1} \end{align*}

Then, we can use this formula to compute the third term:

\begin{align*} a_{3} &= 64 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{3-1} \\[5pt] &= 4^3 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{2} \\[5pt] &= 4^3\cdot \dfrac{1}{4^2} \\[5pt] & = 4^1 \\[5pt] &= 4 \end{align*}

Therefore, the third term is $a_{3} = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ 4}.$

example.title: Finding a Particular Term of a Geometric Sequence Given a Term and the Common Ratio

question.text: Given that the $5$th term of a geometric sequence is $-125$, and the common ratio is $5,$ find the formula for the $n$th term.
question.explanation:
The common ratio is $r = 5,$ so we can start writing the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \\[3pt] &= a_1 \cdot 5^{n-1} \end{align*}

However, we still need to figure out the first term $a_1.$ We know that the $5$th term is $a_5 = -125,$ so we can solve for the first term as follows:

\begin{align*} a_5 & = a_1 \cdot 5^{5-1} \\[3pt] -125 & = a_1 \cdot 5^4 \\[3pt] -5^3 & = a_1 \cdot 5^4 \\[5pt] - \dfrac{1}{5} &= a_1 \end{align*}

Now that we know the first term is $a_1 = - \dfrac{1}{5},$ we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot 5^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= - \dfrac{1}{5} \cdot 5^{n-1} \\[5pt] %&= - \dfrac{1}{5} \cdot 5^{n-1} \\[5pt] & = - \dfrac{5^{n-1}}{5}\\[5pt] &= - 5^{n-2} \end{align*}
